title: Shopping List Organizer with Aisle Ordering
description:
A Python tool that turns a free-text shopping note into a checklist grouped by category and sorted in the order of the aisles in a specific store.

  • Parsing: a rule-based parser reads quantities and units ("2 kg potatoes", "6 eggs"); optionally an LLM via an OpenAI-compatible API parses messy notes such as "stuff for pancakes".
  • Categorization: a keyword table assigns produce, bakery, dairy, pantry and other categories; categories proposed by the LLM are validated against the same list.
  • Aisle ordering: a small JSON file per store lists the categories in walking order.

No shopping, price or store-map APIs are used.
prompts: You turn a shopping note into a JSON object {"items": [{"name": str, "quantity": number, "unit": str or null, "category": str}]}. Allowed categories: produce, bakery, meat_fish, dairy, pantry, beverages, frozen, household, other. Use singular, lowercase English item names. If the note names a dish, list its usual ingredients. Do not invent prices, brands or stores. Answer with JSON only.
implementationSteps: Split the note on commas, new lines and "and", and read quantity and unit with a regular expression
Optionally send the note to an OpenAI-compatible chat model with JSON output, and fall back to the rule parser if the answer is not valid JSON
Categorize items with a keyword table where the last matching keyword wins ("orange juice" is a beverage) and "frozen" overrides
Validate categories returned by the LLM against the allowed list
Merge duplicate items with the same unit, treating singular and plural as one item
Load the store layout JSON and sort the sections in aisle order
Print a checklist; test parser, categorizer, merging, ordering and the LLM path with a fake client
performance: Expectations, not measurements: the rule-based path runs in milliseconds and works offline. The LLM path adds one chat request per note. Categorization quality depends on the keyword table; items it does not know go to "other" instead of being guessed.
userExperience: The user types or pastes a note and gets a checklist with one block per aisle in the order of their store, with quantities merged. Messy notes can be parsed with the optional LLM mode. Changing the store means editing a short list of categories.
